title: More Incidents Don't Necessarily Mean Less Reliability
gist: A Great Circle argument, amplified here, holds that rising incident counts usually signal an improving incident management culture rather than degrading reliability, because incident volume measures willingness to surface problems, not system health. The piece — echoing Sygnia guidance and SLO practice — argues raw counts, ticket volumes and isolated mean-time-to-respond create false confidence, and that treating low incident counts as a KPI actively causes engineers to hide problems.

themes.theme: Incident count measures culture, not reliability

insights.claim: A rising number of reported incidents often indicates an organization's incident management culture is improving, because better processes, tooling, training and operational discipline make teams more willing to formally declare incidents that were previously handled informally or hidden.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: An operational metric that leadership reads as bad news may be evidence of a maturing organization — a direct warning against penalizing engineering teams on incident volume.
insights.quote: an increase in incident counts may actually indicate that an organization's incident management culture is improving
insights.locator: One of the most common assumptions in engineering leadership

insights.claim: Incident count measures an organization's willingness to surface and manage operational problems rather than the underlying reliability of its systems, which makes it unfit for use as a key performance indicator.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Anyone diligencing an engineering organization on incident dashboards is measuring reporting behavior, not service quality — ask for user-impact metrics instead.
insights.quote: Incident count, it argues, measures an organization's willingness to surface and manage operational problems rather than the underlying reliability of its systems.
insights.locator: The article challenges the widespread practice

insights.claim: Mature incident management cultures that push engineers to declare incidents early, involve the right stakeholders and run structured post-incident reviews typically see reported incidents rise initially while simultaneously creating more opportunities to learn and prevent larger outages.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Expect a J-curve after investing in incident tooling — a short-term metric deterioration that should be budgeted for, not corrected.
insights.locator: Mature incident management cultures encourage engineers

insights.claim: The same detection paradox recurs across engineering disciplines: strengthening vulnerability management produces more security findings, better observability produces more alerts, and enhanced testing uncovers more defects, in each case exposing pre-existing problems rather than creating new ones.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A general rule for reading any detection-driven metric: a step-change increase after a tooling investment is evidence the tooling works, not that risk rose.
insights.quote: improved measurement exposes existing problems that were previously invisible rather than creating new ones
insights.locator: The phenomenon is familiar across other engineering disciplines

insights.claim: When engineers stop quietly resolving 'spicy bugs' and degraded services and instead declare formal incidents, dashboards show more incidents while the organization has actually become more resilient by making operational knowledge visible and repeatable.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Resilience gains show up as worse-looking dashboards; the diagnostic is whether knowledge is being captured, not whether the count fell.
insights.locator: Incident management follows the same pattern

insights.claim: Modern SRE practice has shifted away from simplistic operational metrics toward customer impact, recovery effectiveness and organizational learning — replacing 'How many incidents occurred?' with how quickly users were affected, how rapidly service was restored, whether root cause was identified, and whether similar failures are becoming less frequent.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A ready-made four-question replacement scorecard for evaluating an engineering org's reliability posture.
insights.locator: This perspective aligns with broader thinking

insights.claim: Recent Sygnia guidance argues that raw incident counts, ticket volumes and even mean time to respond viewed in isolation create false confidence because they measure operational activity rather than organizational readiness, and recommends containment effectiveness, escalation quality, post-incident improvements and incident response process maturity instead.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Even MTTR — the metric most boards still trust — is called out as misleading in isolation; security and reliability guidance are converging on readiness measures.
insights.quote: can create false confidence because they measure operational activity rather than organizational readiness

insights.claim: Reliability practices built around Service Level Objectives increasingly emphasize user-centric measures such as error budget burn, SLI degradation and customer impact over infrastructure-centric statistics like raw uptime.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Demand for SLO/error-budget tooling follows from this shift; infrastructure-uptime-centric monitoring vendors are on the wrong side of it.
insights.locator: Likewise, modern reliability practices built around Service Level Objectives

themes.theme: Metric pressure as a failure mode

insights.claim: If engineers believe they will be judged on keeping incident counts low, they will delay declaring incidents, try to resolve problems alone, or avoid escalating emerging issues until they become significantly worse — reducing organizational visibility exactly when rapid collaboration matters most.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: A textbook Goodhart effect with operational consequences: targeting the incident metric converts small incidents into large outages.
insights.quote: Organizations should avoid discouraging incident declarations simply to improve dashboard metrics.
insights.locator: Perhaps the most important message from Great Circle

insights.claim: Healthy engineering organizations reward transparency by treating an incident declaration as the beginning of a structured learning process rather than an admission of failure, so operational knowledge accumulates over time instead of remaining trapped within individual responders.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: Knowledge trapped in individual responders is a concentration risk in any engineering org; blameless process is what converts it into an institutional asset.
insights.locator: Instead, healthy engineering organizations reward transparency

insights.claim: A falling incident count is ambiguous evidence: it may indicate improving reliability, but it could equally suggest under-reporting, inconsistent classification, or a weakening incident culture.
insights.speaker: Craig Risi
insights.so_what: The single most actionable takeaway for anyone reading an engineering scorecard — a declining incident trend requires corroboration before being read as good news.
insights.quote: A falling incident count may indicate improving reliability, but it could equally suggest under-reporting, inconsistent classification, or a weakening incident culture.
insights.locator: The broader lesson is that metrics should reflect the outcomes
